lesson.grammar_point: hedging: tentative claims (may, be likely to, seem to, suggest that)

vocab.title: Match each word to its meaning
defs: to describe the main points of something, without the details
to make something bad less serious or less harmful
to speak formally to a group of people, or to deal with a problem
the quality of being honest and reliable; in a market, being trustworthy
strong and reliable; able to resist being questioned
a person or a group with an interest in a project or a decision
a weakness in a rule that lets people avoid it legally
a formal public promise, often made by a country or a company

items.situation: An investor asks: "Will carbon prices go up next year?"
tips: They are likely to rise, but it depends on the new rules.
be likely to: a forecast, not a promise.

items.situation: Another asks: "Are all Brazilian credits reliable?"
tips: Most of them seem to be robust, but some projects may have weak baselines.
seem to + verb; may for a possible problem.

items.situation: Someone asks: "Is there a loophole in the new rules?"
tips: There appears to be one in how land use is counted.
there appears to be: it probably exists.

items.situation: Daniel asks: "What does the data show?"
tips: The data suggests that buyers are becoming more careful.
suggests that, with no person after suggest.

items.situation: A journalist asks: "Will companies meet their pledges?"
tips: Many will, but projects tend to take longer than planned.

items.situation: Daniel asks: "Your position, in one sentence?"
tips: Our position is clear: without integrity, the market will not recover.
the main point has no hedge.

listenings.text: Good afternoon. I will be brief, because the negotiations are still going on. Three points. First, on carbon markets, we have made progress, but it is too early to say that we have an agreement. The text that was published this morning is likely to change again tonight. Second, several countries have asked for stronger rules on integrity. The evidence suggests that buyers will not return to the market until the rules are robust, and we agree with that. Third, on finance, the pledges that were made last year have not been fully delivered. It seems that some countries are waiting for the final text before they commit more money. We may see new announcements on Thursday, but I would not expect large numbers. I will take two questions.

When lawyers speak at an international forum, they often make one of two mistakes. The first is to sound too certain. If you say that a project will remove one million tons of carbon, somebody in the room will ask you to prove it, and you probably cannot. The second mistake is the opposite: to hedge everything. If every sentence starts with perhaps, or it might be possible that, the audience stops listening, because they cannot find your position. So use a simple structure. Start with your point, in one sentence, with no hedge. Then give the evidence, and this is where hedging belongs: the data suggests, the numbers seem to show. Then explain the impact: who is affected, and how. And finish with a recommendation, clear and short. Point, evidence, impact, recommendation. One hedge for each claim is enough. Two hedges in the same sentence sound like fear.

extra_audio.text: First, thank the moderator and say who you are. Then state your point in one sentence, with no hedge. Then give the evidence, with a careful verb such as suggests. Then explain the impact: who is affected, and how. And finally, finish with a clear recommendation.
